summary: Defines FLUTE, File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport, a protocol for sending files one way over the Internet, especially suited to multicast networks. It builds on Asynchronous Layered Coding, the base protocol for massively scalable multicast distribution. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Like a radio tower broadcasting a file to many listeners at once, FLUTE sends the same file to everyone without needing each listener to talk back.

questions: how to deliver files over multicast
how does flute deliver files over multicast
what is a file delivery table
subtitle: How to broadcast files to many receivers at once, with no feedback channel, by sending a table that describes each file.

tldr.problem: Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) can carry arbitrary binary objects to many receivers, but a receiver also needs to know what each object is: its name, type, size and encoding.
tldr.mechanism: FLUTE sends a File Delivery Table (FDT), an XML description of each file, in-band as special objects with TOI 0, and maps every file to a TOI inside an ALC session.
tldr.outcome: This is FLUTE version 2 on the Standards Track. It obsoletes the experimental FLUTE version 1 of RFC 3926 and is not backwards compatible with it.

today: RFC 6726 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It obsoletes the experimental FLUTE of RFC 3926, and it is not backwards compatible with that version.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6726 defines FLUTE, File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport. It is a protocol for one-way delivery of files over the Internet and is particularly suited to multicast networks. It builds on Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC, RFC 5775), the base protocol designed for massively scalable multicast distribution.

ALC transports arbitrary binary objects, but for file delivery that is not enough: the end systems need to know what the objects represent. FLUTE adds a way to signal and map the properties of files onto ALC concepts. It also adds a file delivery session with timing constraints, in-band signaling of the session's transport parameters, in-band signaling of file properties, and rules for multiplexing several files in one session.

The RFC says FLUTE suits delivering large and small files to many hosts over sessions of several seconds or more, for example large software updates, segmented data such as time-lined subtitle text, or metadata such as SDP files. It works with multicast and unicast, but its primary use is unidirectional multicast. It requires connectivity from sender to receivers, not from receivers back to the sender. FLUTE does not give senders a way to verify that receivers got the files; the RFC leaves such a method out of scope.
sections.eli5: Imagine a teacher shouting a lesson to a whole school yard. FLUTE is the rule book that says how to also shout which page each part belongs to, so everybody can put the lesson together.

sections.title: The File Delivery Session
sections.content:
A FLUTE session is an ALC/LCT session. It is made of channels from a single sender. A session is identified by the pair (source IP address, Transport Session Identifier), where the TSI is an integer carried in a field of 16, 32 or 48 bits. Inside the session, each object has a Transmission Object Identifier (TOI). An object is either a file or an FDT Instance.

The rules for TOI values are simple. The TOI field MUST be present in FLUTE packets, with one exception: a packet that carries no payload and has the Close Session flag set to 1 SHALL NOT carry it. TOI 0 is reserved for FDT Instances. Every file MUST be associated with a TOI greater than 0 within the session.

A FLUTE session under this document MUST use FLUTE version 2, ALC version 1 and LCT version 1. The FLUTE version travels in the EXT_FDT header extension. Because not every packet carries that extension, a new receiver may need to wait until it arrives before knowing the version.
sections.eli5: Each broadcast has a channel name and every file in it gets a number tag. Number 0 is always the table of contents.

sections.title: The File Delivery Table
sections.content:
The core of FLUTE is the File Delivery Table (FDT). Logically it is a set of file description entries, one per file. Each entry MUST include the TOI of the file and a URI that identifies it. Entries can also carry the media type, the size, the content encoding, a message digest, and the FEC Object Transmission Information.

On the wire, the FDT is sent as FDT Instances. An FDT Instance is an XML document with a single root element FDT-Instance, and it MUST have an Expires attribute. Each file is a File child element, which MUST contain at least TOI and Content-Location. Other attributes reuse HTTP header names: Content-Type, Content-Length, Content-Encoding and Content-MD5. Transfer-Length carries the length of the object as transported, which differs from the file length when content encoding such as compression is applied.

An optional Complete attribute, when true, says that this instance lists every file delivered so far and every file still to come. A receiver that has not seen it must assume new files may still be announced. Attributes set on FDT-Instance apply to all its files, and the same attribute on a File element takes precedence. The RFC says Content-MD5 is for integrity of the decoded object and MUST NOT be regarded as a security mechanism.
sections.eli5: The table is a packing list. For each parcel it says its number, its name, what kind of thing it is, and how big it should be, so you can check you got it all.

sections.title: How FDT Instances Behave
sections.content:
Every file delivered MUST have an entry in at least one FDT Instance. Instances can appear anywhere in a session and can be interleaved with file packets. Instances can overlap, repeat, or add to one another, but later instances MUST NOT change parameters already described for a TOI. It is RECOMMENDED that the entry for a file be sent at least once before the file itself, so receivers need not buffer or discard file data that arrives early. The RFC notes this cannot be fully guaranteed because the first FDT transmission can be lost.

An FDT Instance is valid until its expiration time. The time is a 32-bit unsigned integer, the 32 most significant bits of a 64-bit NTP time value, in seconds since 1 January 1900. Senders MUST set an expiry in the future, and receivers MUST NOT use an instance to interpret packets after it expires. The RFC explains how to pick the right 136-year NTP epoch for the 2036 wraparound by choosing the one closest to the current time.

Because file recovery depends on the FDT, senders SHOULD assume receivers will miss some FDT packets. The RFC recommends that file attributes be delivered with a higher probability than file recovery. An FDT Instance longer than one packet payload should use an FEC code that protects against loss. The default is Compact No-Code FEC Encoding ID 0.
sections.eli5: The packing list can go out of date, so each copy has an expiry time. Because mail can get lost, you keep sending copies of the list before and during the files.

sections.title: The EXT_FDT and EXT_CENC Headers
sections.content:
FDT Instances travel in ALC packets with TOI 0 and a required LCT header extension, EXT_FDT. It is a fixed-length 32-bit extension with Header Extension Type (HET) 192. It has a 4-bit FLUTE version field V, which MUST be 2, and a 20-bit FDT Instance ID.

Instance IDs start at 0 and go up by one for each new instance. After reaching 2^20-1 the numbering wraps to the smallest ID of an expired instance, and the wrapped value counts as logically higher. Senders MUST NOT reuse an ID that belongs to a non-expired instance. Receivers MUST be ready for wraparound and for gaps in the numbering.

An FDT Instance can itself be compressed or otherwise content encoded. In that case the EXT_CENC extension, HET 193, MUST be present in all packets of that instance, together with EXT_FDT. It holds an 8-bit encoding value followed by 16 reserved bits, which MUST be zero. Values 0, 1, 2 and 3 are reserved for null, ZLIB, DEFLATE and GZIP.
sections.eli5: Each copy of the packing list gets a small sticker with a version number, and, if the list was squashed to save space, a second sticker saying how it was squashed.

sections.title: Channels, FEC Information and Session Setup
sections.content:
FLUTE envisions four setups: one or several channels, each with or without congestion control supplied by ALC. Without ALC congestion control is allowed only in a controlled network where flow and congestion control come from other means. With several channels, one object may finish before an object that started earlier. If an application needs strict ordering, the RFC recommends a single channel. FDT packets SHOULD NOT be biased toward layers that low-rate receivers do not join.

FEC Object Transmission Information MUST be delivered in-band, either with the ALC extension EXT_FTI or in the FDT through attributes such as FEC-OTI-FEC-Encoding-ID and FEC-OTI-Max-Number-of-Encoding-Symbols. The information must be identical whichever way it is delivered, and receivers should prefer EXT_FTI when both are present. The FEC Encoding ID of a file MUST be carried in the Codepoint field of the ALC/LCT header.

Before receiving, a receiver must know the source IP address, the number of channels, the destination address and port of each channel, the TSI, and that the session is a FLUTE session. The RFC does not say how receivers learn these. It suggests a session description such as SDP, fetched by some other means, and leaves the choice open. Appendix A gives an informative receiver loop: join channels, check the TSI, demultiplex by TOI, recover objects, update the FDT database from instances, and apply file properties to recovered files.
sections.eli5: You can listen on one radio channel or several. Several channels let slow listeners and fast listeners both join in, but then files may finish in a different order than they started.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists attacks on the data flow, the session description, the FDT Instances, the ALC/LCT header fields, and the congestion control building block. Confidentiality is normally provided by encrypting the whole file before FEC, or per packet, for example with IPsec/ESP. For file corruption, it recommends that at least one integrity and sender authentication technique be used.

The RFC compares file-level signatures, per-packet signatures, a group-keyed MAC such as HMAC-SHA-256, TESLA, and IPsec/ESP. File-level checks are cheap but cannot tell good packets from bad ones. Per-packet checks can, at extra cost. A group-keyed MAC only proves group membership, since every member can forge packets. Forged packets with the Close Session flag set can make a receiver quit early, and a corrupted FDT can make a receiver reject good files or use costly FEC settings.

For minimum security, FLUTE inherits the baseline from ALC: IPsec/ESP in transport mode, which is mandatory to implement but not necessarily to use. It gives per-packet data origin authentication, integrity verification and anti-replay, and per-packet encryption SHOULD be added if confidentiality is needed.
sections.eli5: If someone can shout fake pages into the broadcast, receivers might throw away good files. So the sender should sign or lock the messages so receivers can tell real ones from fakes.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA took five actions for this document. It registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:fdt, registered the FDT Instance XML schema, and registered the media type application/fdt+xml, whose file extension is .fdt. It created a new FLUTE Content Encoding Algorithms registry with values 0 to 255, using the Specification Required policy. Finally it registered two LCT header extension types, 192 for EXT_FDT and 193 for EXT_CENC.
sections.eli5: The rule makers wrote the new names and numbers into the official phone book so nobody else uses them by accident.

fields.desc: Identifies the FDT Instance within the session.

data.title: FDT Instance
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<FDT-Instance xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
  xsi:schemaLocation="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:fdt
                      ietf-flute-fdt.xsd"
  Expires="2890842807">
  <File
    Content-Location="http://www.example.com/menu/tracklist.html"
    TOI="1"
    Content-Type="text/html"/>
  <File
    Content-Location="http://www.example.com/tracks/track1.mp3"
    TOI="2"
    Content-Length="6100"
    Content-Type="audio/mp3"
    Content-Encoding="gzip"
    Content-MD5="+VP5IrWploFkZWc11iLDdA=="
    Some-Private-Extension-Tag="abc123"/>
</FDT-Instance>
